The material is uniformly straw/tan colored with no green remaining — suggesting either complete plant death from a systemic disease, or dried ear husks from an ear rot. The background shows a dried corn field.

Key observations:
- Material appears to be dried corn leaf/husk tissue
- Uniform tan/straw coloration — no green
- No visible mold, lesions, or distinctive patterns on the dried tissue
- Collected in a bag (field sampling context)

The material resembles dried corn husks. Let me view the Ear_rots_Diplodia reference, as Diplodia causes premature drying and bleaching of husks.

**Analysis:**

The Ear_rots_Diplodia reference shows characteristic dried, bleached corn husks — the papery, tan/straw-colored strips are very similar to the material collected in the test image bag. Diplodia ear rot is known for causing premature drying and bleaching of husks, and the top-left panel of the reference clearly shows the same elongated, straw-colored, papery husk strips as seen in the test image.

The dried field background in the test image is also consistent with a late-season ear rot sampling scenario. The material appears to be stripped corn husks collected for disease assessment.

The match to Diplodia is reasonable given:
- Uniformly tan/straw bleached husk tissue
- No green remaining (premature senescence)
- Papery texture consistent with Diplodia-affected husks
- Late-season field context
